item.title: Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
item.description: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales. item.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
item.description: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson . While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago. item.title: ULA says Vulcan lacked the oomph to get Amazon satellites to orbit
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight. ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. Howeve

item.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
item.description: null NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later. "The Earth and Voyager are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light," Voyager Project Scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com. "It's a very special moment where Voyager 1 is about 16.1 billion miles away, and we're celebrating that moment because it's the first human-made object to actually reach one light-day distance." All things Voyager The two Voyager spacecraft have been on one serious ride since launching in 1977. And each of these twin probes has taken a unique and historic journey through our solar system and beyond. On Voyager 1's trip through our cosmic neighborhood, for example, it made countless groundbreaking observations of planets and moons that we had never before seen up close (or at all). The probe discovered a ring around Jupiter as well as the planet's moons Thebe and Metis. It also found five new moons and a new ring around Saturn. "Voyager 1 flew past the Jupiter system and took images of Jupiter's moon Io, and it actually discovered that Io is volcanically active. So, images that were taken showed these volcanoes that were actively erupting, and we learned that Io is actually the most volcanically active body in our solar system, which is just amazing," Cynthia Phillips, a project scientist for NASA's Europa Clipper mission, told Space.com about one of Voyager 1's many discoveries. The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes both flew past Jupiter in 1979, on their way out of the solar system. Represented here is Voyager 2's encounter with Jupiter. NASA/JPL A close-up of Jupiter's Great Red Spot as seen by one of NASA's Voyager spacecraft. NASA/JPL-Caltech Voyager 1 took photos of Jupiter and two of its satellites (Io, left, and Europa). The new study says that moons orbiting a gas giant planet greater than 8 Jupiter masses could help astronomers detect a rogue planet. NASA/JPL A mosaic of Jupiter by Voyager 1. JPL Jupiter and two of its moons — Io, to the left, and Europa — as seen by Voyager 1 on Feb. 13, 1979. JPL/NASA Voyager 1 image of Jupiter's volcanic moon Io, showing the active plume of a volcano called Loki. item.title: Beyoncé Becomes First Artist in Grammy History to Earn 100 Nominations!
item.description: Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “ Morning Dew ( Donk )”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys). Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani , Victoria Monét , Jill Scott , and Nigerian star Tems . To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z , at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history. Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack. Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti ’s 31 trophies. She pushed that tally even higher at the 2025 Grammys, taking home three awards—Album of the Year and Best Country Album for Cowboy Carter, as well as Best Country Duo/Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” alongside Miley Cyrus . Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36. item.title: UK.gov JV gets £178M Home Office hosting deal. Without competition
item.description: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure. According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
item.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
item.description: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. item.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
item.description: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. item.title: From Bronze-Brown Traditional Attire to Bridal Lace, See Tomi Thomas & Efya’s Wedding Looks
item.description: Newlyweds Efya and Tomi Thomas at their white wedding reception in Accra. Photo Credit: Thret Studio/Instagram Two music stars, two countries, one beautiful love story! Nigerian singer Tomi Thomas and Ghanaian songstress Efya have made things official, celebrating their union in Accra with a wedding that brought Nigerian and Ghanaian traditions together. From their coordinated traditional looks to their elegant white wedding outfits and a song Tomi made especially for his bride, there was plenty to love about this celebration. If you’ve followed the music scenes in Nigeria and Ghana, you’ll know that Tomi and Efya have each carved out their own place in contemporary African music. Tomi Thomas, who hails from Delta State, Nigeria, first gained recognition as part of the music collective L.O.S (Loud On Sound), before building a solo catalogue that moves across Afro-fusion and alternative sounds. Efya, born Jane Awindor in Kumasi, Ghana, is one of the country’s most celebrated vocalists, known for her soulful music and multiple Ghana Music Awards. Now, the two have added a beautiful new chapter to their story, bringing their families, friends and two cultures together in Accra. Efya and Tomi Thomas in black and olive-green outfits for their wedding reception. Photo Credit: Photo Humor/Instagram One of the lovely fashion moments from the celebration was their Nigerian traditional attire. The couple coordinated in rich bronze-brown shades, with Tomi wearing a woven traditional robe, complete with a matching traditional cap. He accessorised with layered orange coral neck beads, matching wrist beads and black loafers, while carrying a circular feathered fan inscribed with “OGENEE”. Efya was every bit his match in a fitted, floor-length bronze-brown gown, with gold and silver beadwork covering the corset bodice and sheer sleeves. The structured peplum details at the hips added shape to the dress, while a beaded treble clef motif on the skirt made a sweet reference to the music that brought so much of their story together. She finished with a pleated gold-and-bronze headwrap, a white-and-coral beaded choker, coral earrings and gold strappy heels. Tomi Thomas and Efya in coordinated bronze-brown traditional attire for their wedding in Accra. Photo Credit: Tomi Thomas/Instagram For their white wedding, the couple opted for a timeless black-and-white palette. Tomi kept things classic in a double-breasted white tuxedo jacket, complete with a white pocket square, crisp dress shirt and black bow tie. Black tailored trousers and matching dress shoes completed his look. Efya, meanwhile, made a beautiful bridal entrance in a fitted white lace mermaid gown with an embellished illusion neckline, sheer floral lace long sleeves and a corset-style waist. The voluminous detachable overskirt added another dimension to the dress, while her sleek low bun and large white structured bouquet with a jewelled centre completed her bridal look. item.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
item.description: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. item.title: Detty December 2026 Travel Guide: Hotels, Resorts and Things to Do in Lagos and Enugu
item.description: December in Nigeria is practically a season of its own. Group chats are buzzing, flights are being booked, wedding invitations are coming in, an everyone seems to have holiday plans. From concerts, parties, and social gatherings to family reunions and Christmas celebrations, there is always something happening. For many, it is the most anticipated time of the year, a chance to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and make the most of the holidays. For some, it’s the excitement of Detty December in Lagos. For others, it’s finally getting everyone together for Christmas, taking a much-needed break, or planning a getaway after a long year. With so much happening, one thing deserves a little more attention than it usually gets: where you’ll be staying. A good hotel can make all the difference to your holiday. Think relaxing mornings, comfortable rooms, good food, a convenient location, exciting experiences nearby, and somewhere to unwind after a long day of activities. After all, where you stay can shape your entire holiday experience. Whether you’re planning to experience Detty December in Lagos or spend Christmas in Enugu, we’ve put together a guide to some accommodation options and experiences worth considering as you plan your holiday. Where to Stay in Lagos for Detty December Anyone who has experienced Lagos in December knows that the city takes the festive season seriously. Concerts, weddings, parties, restaurant dates, beach outings, family gatherings and the occasional last-minute plan that turns into the highlight of your holiday, there’s always something happening. With so much going on across the city, staying in a convenient location can save you time and make getting around much easier. Victoria Island remains one of Lagos’s most popular areas for visitors during the festive season, thanks to its restaurants, entertainment destinations, and proximity to major lifestyl attractions; it’s a top pick for visitors looking for the best of the city in December. A top hotel choice located in Landmark Lagos, Oniru, Victoria Island would be the Landmark Hotel, which offers an appealing option for visitors looking to enjoy the best of Lagos while having a comfortable place to retreat to at the end of the day. With ocean and city views, comfortable accommodation and access to the wider Landmark Lagos leisure and lifestyle ecosystem, Landmark Hotel gives guests more than just a place to stay. It puts them close to a range of experiences, dining options and entertainment destinations, making it easier to enjoy the festive season without having to travel too far. And the best part? There’s plenty to explore! Guests can enjoy dining experiences within the Landmark ecosystem, visit the Landmark Upside Down House, and attend events at POP Landmark, Landmark Center, or simply spend time exploring the recreational attractions available in the area. item.title: Tochukwu Ekoh: What My Friend’s Passing Taught Me About Kindness
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way . We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? Why did we have to start talking, sharing experiences and becoming familiar with each other again, only for him to die shortly afterwards? Why him? Why at that particular time? What was the reason for that reconnection, and why did it have to end this way? The timing of certain events leaves you with more questions than answers. What makes this loss even more difficult to comprehend is how it happened. I had been the one who suffered an accident, yet I survived and was gradually recovering. He wasn’t sick. He hadn’t been involved in an accident. He simply slipped and fell, sustained an injury, and bled out. His body was not discovered until three days later. Three days. The loneliness he must have experienced within those three days, the possibility that he needed someone, and the heartbreaking thought that nobody knew what had happened to him. I cannot fully comprehend it. It also made me confront something I had perhaps never

item.title: Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action
item.description: I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology. A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage. To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements. Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do. That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes. Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages. I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done. But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements. If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity. Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®

item.title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype
item.description: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet . Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters. When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe. The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo , who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming. AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool. Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall. Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator . That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed? Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less." What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it. I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA 's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month. My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.” Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation. item.title: Temu's compliance regime is low-quality, fits badly, and full of holes, says Europe
item.description: Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations. The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps. Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including: Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports; Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks; Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety; Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu; When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores; Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores. A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings. "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns." The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine. Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods. This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions. Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retail

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 18 – A Medium-Sized Solar Flare
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. item.title: Sierra Snow Season Spins Up
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Sierra Snow Season Spins Up Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 Curtain Toggle 2-Up California’s Sierra Nevada got an early taste of wintry weather when one of the first major snowfalls of the water year arrived on November 13, 2026. A moisture-laden storm delivered heavy rains to lower elevations in the Sacramento area and snow accumulations of around a foot to some mountainous areas. The recent bout of wet weather was the first in a quick succession of Pacific storms bringing rain, snow, and wind to the U.S. West in mid-November. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image (right) of fresh snow in the Sierra Nevada on the morning of November 14, during a lull between weather systems. Two days earlier (left), the mountains were mostly bare, with snow appearing only at the highest elevations. Nearly 12 inches (30 centimeters) of snow fell at Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, on November 13, according to the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory . The accumulation snarled traffic on Interstate 80 in the area, prompting officials to close the highway in both directions that evening. To the south, the ski resort at Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 centimeters) of new snow, and officials at Yosemite National Park closed several roads ahead of the storm. More wet weather and mountain snow are forecast to follow . The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a winter storm warning for portions of the Sierras above 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) in elevation from November 18 to 20. NWS warned of difficult-to-impossible travel conditions, gusty winds, and snow accumulations of around 4 feet (120 centimeters) possible above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters). NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview . Story by Lindsey Doermann. item.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
item.description: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. item.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
item.description: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. item.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
item.description: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfor

item.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
item.description: At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC). The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028. According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities. This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads. “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg . “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.” Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community. Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions. The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists. When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well. Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains. Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation. We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme. The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance. Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS. While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation. item.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
item.description: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
item.description: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight. “As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!” Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space. Judges Needed NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website . item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
item.description: null Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9. The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much. "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote . "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure." item.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
item.description: 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Two NASA Space Apps Challenge participants in Vilhena, Brazil work together during the annual hackathon on their project submission. NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries. The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration. Participants join events organized by local volunteers to work in teams and address one of the challenges and submit their project before the deadline. Projects are then judged to determine 10 global winners, to be announced in January. “The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.” One of the local winning teams from NASA Space Apps Challenge NYC pose with volunteer local lead Nate Cooper. NASA Challenges also feature data from 17 international space agency partners, all Artemis Accord signatories. This year’s space agency partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office (GGPEN), Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency (AEB), CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina (CONAE), Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency. Three agencies, GGPEN, AEB, and CONAE, also wrote challenges this year. To learn more about NASA’s Space Apps Challenge, visit: spaceappschallenge.org Karen Fox / Jessica Hall Headquarters, Washington karen.c.fox@nasa.gov / jessica.hall@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 18, 2026 Related Terms Open Science Explore More 4 min read NASA Welcomes All Ages, Experience Levels for Space Apps Challenge Article 1 month ago 4 min read NASA’s Prithvi Becomes First AI Geos

item.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. item.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
item.description: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. item.title: Bitcoin Price Slips Below $64,000 as Strategy (MSTR) Falls Below $100
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Slips Below $64,000 as Strategy (MSTR) Falls Below $100 Bitcoin price slipped near $64,000 on Tuesday afternoon, as Strategy (MSTR) and Coinbase (COIN) shares fell and traders waited on Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. The bitcoin price had climbed back to about $65,000 before the U.S. open, after holding near that level on Monday. Selling picked up once stocks turned lower, and bitcoin price slipped to about $63,300 at its low. Strategy and Coinbase shares slide Strategy shares were recently down more than 5% to about $97, dropping below $100 and trading under the company’s STRC preferred stock, which was little changed near $99. It is the first time the common has traded below the preferred since mid-August. The stock is also down about 20% from its Nov. 10 close near $121. Strategy added 485 bitcoin last week, lifting its holdings to 850,849 BTC. The shares have kept falling with the bitcoin price. Coinbase was recently down about 3% to about $116. Robinhood (HOOD) and Circle (CRCL) dropped about 4% and 5%. Bitcoin miners were mostly lower. MARA Holdings (MARA), CleanSpark (CLSK) and IREN (IREN) each fell about 3% to 4%, and Cipher Mining (CIFR) was down about 2%. Hut 8 (HUT) was a modest exception, recently up about 1%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) were little changed, while Core Scientific (CORZ) and BitMine (BMNR) were also lower. Nvidia earnings weigh on stocks The broader market was also weaker late in the session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was recently down about 1.7%, after falling as much as about 1,000 points, or 2%, at its session low. The S&P 500 was down about 1.2% and the Nasdaq Composite about 1%. Nvidia shares were recently down about 1.4%, after falling more than 3% earlier in the session. The chipmaker reports results after the bell, with analysts expecting revenue of about $109 billion. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead her first earnings call in the role. Huang, in his first public statement since resigning last week, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and America. Sources told CNBC on Monday that the board is not considering bringing him back. The bitcoin price bounced from its low as Nvidia shares pared some of their losses, and was recently near $64,000. What comes next for the bitcoin price New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that the AI investment boom could mean “we may need to raise rates more.” He played down a half-point hike in December. “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action,” Williams said. Fed Governor Christopher Waller did not address the December decision in a payments speech Tuesday. Last week, he said a half-point hike should be considered if October’s core inflation ran at 0.3% or higher, and it did. Markets still point to a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting. item.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
item.description: null A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test. London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite , at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles). The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent. Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector, which is designed to help trackers keep tabs on satellites in orbit. It recently passed its first in-space test. (Image credit: Foundational) The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft. The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit. Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit . "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks." Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector is seen before its July 2026 launch. The device is attached to its cubesat, which itself is integrated into one of D-Orbit's ION carrier craft. (Image credit: Foundational) Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month.
